Its members are delegates of the sixteen Land governments, appointed and recallable by them. Article 51(3) of the Basic Law requires each Land to cast its votes einheitlich as a bloc and the chamber has no Fraktionen (no party affiliations).
There is therefore no party field, and its absence is a design decision rather than a gap: the operative political unit is territorial. Every contribution carries the Bundesland it was made for, which makes territorial representation and federal–state conflict directly measurable from text. # The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
## 1 Background & Summary
Despite significant importance of the political discourse within the Bundesrat in the national politics, to the best of authors’ knowledge, there exists no corpus dataset of the Bundesrat. The 1,067 plenary sittings since 1949 exist only as PDF documents on the chamber’s official website. The 1949–-1999 portion of the corpus includes roughly 27,000 pages that exists only as scanned images, with no text layer at all.
To address the aforementioned data gap, in this Data Descriptor, we present a complete speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber’s first sitting on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. It comprises 53,362 speeches delivered in the chamber including written statements.
## 2 Methods
### 2.2 Data Source
It is published in different period-based web pages (e.g., 1949–1950, 1951–1955, …, 2026–2030) as PDF documents. Each PDF document represents one session and the filename carries useful information, including session number and date that are essential for building the metadata. ## Description

Structured, speaker-attributed corpus of all German Bundesrat (Federal Council) plenary session transcripts (Plenarprotokolle) from the chamber's first sitting to the present (sessions 1–1067, September 1949 – July 2026). Every attributed contribution is extracted from the official PDFs published by the Bundesrat and linked to the speaker's name, resolved person identity, official role, gender, and Bundesland (Federal State) the speaker represents.

**Scale:** 1,067 sessions · 53,362 attributed contributions (47,290 spoken in the chamber, 6,072 submitted in writing) · 2,473 identified persons · 76 years of proceedings

**Why this chamber is different**

The Bundesrat is not a second elected chamber. Its members are delegates of the sixteen Land governments, appointed and recallable by them. Article 51(3) of the Basic Law requires each Land to cast its votes _einheitlich_ as a bloc and the chamber has no _Fraktionen_ (no party affiliations). There is therefore no party field, and its absence is a design decision rather than a gap: the operative political unit is territorial. Every contribution carries the Bundesland it was made for, which makes territorial representation and federal–state conflict directly measurable from text.

The chamber is also permanent, never dissolved, no elections, continuous session numbering since 1949 so the corpus is a single unbroken series rather than one segmented by legislative period.

keenable.title: Bundesrecht: An Open Library and Corpus for German Statutory Reference Processing
keenable.snippet: Existing tools for German focus either on parsing references from legal documents or accessing statutory text once citations are explicit. This paper introduces bundesrecht, an open resource for German statutory reference processing, consisting of a software library and a structured corpus of German federal law. The library parses, normalizes, and resolves German statutory references, mapping raw citation strings to structured objects, expanding compact references into canonical forms, and linking them to statutory provisions. The accompanying dataset preserves the internal hierarchy of statutes from laws to fine-granular subclauses. We evaluate the parser and normalizer on 2,944 annotated German legal references using strict exact-match and micro information extraction metrics. We further evaluate canonical reference deduplication and show that normalized references group real citation surface variants far more reliably than string matching. bundesrecht is the first open resource that covers German statutory reference processing as an end-to-end pipeline, from raw citation string to resolved statutory provision, and is available on PyPI.

One of the two legislative chambers of the German **Reich**. The Bundesrat represented the 20 states, as well as the three free cities and held considerable power when it came to the passage of laws, the formulation of policy, and the dissolving of the Reichstag. The Bundesrat epitomized the federal element of the Reich constitution and was especially designed to guard against parliamentarianism. At its inception in 1871, the Bundesrat was the highest constitutional body of the Empire. Modeled on the constitution of the North German Confederation, the Bundesrat was intended by Bismarck as a hybrid between legislature and executive. In practice, however, its main function was to make, not to implement, laws. All legislative proposals were first introduced in the Bundesrat. Only if the upper house approved of the proposal would the bill be passed on to the popularly elected Reichstag. Apart from making law, the Bundesrat decided on a possible declaration of war as well as over constitutional quarrels among the member states of the Reich.

   In the Bundesrat, the otherwise obvious Prussian hegemony was disguised. Although the kingdom made up nearly two-thirds of the Empire’s population and territory, it disposed of only 17 of a total of 58 votes (61 after the reform of 1911). Next to Prussia, Bavaria had six, Saxony and Wurttemberg four, and Hesse and Bade three votes each. The other votes were distributed among the smaller states, many of them enclaves surrounded by Prussian territory. Accordingly, Prussia wielded an often overwhelming influence in the chamber.

## Introduction

The Bundesrat is a pivotal institution within the Federal Republic of Germany, serving as the upper house of parliament and representing the sixteen Länder (federal states) at the national level. Alongside the Bundestag, it plays a crucial role in the legislative process. The Bundesrat provides a platform for the states to influence federal legislation, ensuring that regional interests are integrated into national policies. This body is integral to Germany's system of cooperative federalism, where both federal and state governments collaborate closely to govern the country effectively. ## Abstract
The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

Structured, speaker-attributed corpus of all German Bundesrat (Federal Council) plenary session transcripts (Plenarprotokolle) from the chamber's first sitting to the present (sessions 1–1067, September 1949 – July 2026). Every attributed contribution is extracted from the official PDFs published by the Bundesrat and linked to the speaker's name, resolved person identity, official role, gender, and Bundesland (Federal State) the speaker represents.
Source PDFs are the official protocols from the Bundesrat's archive (bundesrat.de). Two document generations are covered: 747 sessions (1949–1999) survive only as page images and were recovered by OCR (Tesseract, German), roughly 27,000 pages released in machine-readable form here for the first time; 320 sessions (2000–2026) carry a PDF text layer read with pdftotext.
Unlike the Bundestag, the Bundesrat has no official biographical register, its members sit for Land governments and are absent from the Bundestag Stammdaten.

The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.
